question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old man arrives in the pre-operative bay this morning for an elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy to remove a chronically inflamed segment containing a large, non-dysplastic sessile adenoma that could not be lifted for endoscopic resection; the colorectal surgeons anticipate a four-port technique, two to three hours of pneumoperitoneum, and conversion to an open approach only if dense adhesions are encountered, with postoperative transfer to the monitored surgical ward. He ambulated into the facility without assistance, places his own overnight bag on the stretcher, and engages staff with detailed questions about enhanced-recovery pathways, explaining that he continues to walk two miles daily around his neighborhood and climbs a flight of stairs at home several times a day without dyspnea or leg discomfort. His recent medical course, however, has been eventful: twenty-six days ago he presented to an outside emergency department febrile to 38.9 °C with productive cough and right-lower-lobe crackles; chest radiography demonstrated a focal infiltrate consistent with community-acquired pneumonia for which he completed a seven-day course of oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and is now afebrile with clear lung fields on auscultation. Fourteen days after that infection began—twelve days before today—he developed substernal pressure while pruning hedges, called emergency services promptly, and was found to have an elevated high-sensitivity troponin with new T-wave inversions in leads V4–V6; coronary angiography revealed a focal 70 % stenosis in the mid-left anterior descending artery that was successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent, and dual antiplatelet therapy of aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg was initiated. Cardiology follow-up four days ago cleared him for the planned bowel surgery because his left ventricular ejection fraction is preserved at 60 %, he has had no recurrent chest discomfort, and recent exercise tolerance remains excellent. Past medical history is otherwise notable only for well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine and a genetically confirmed heterozygous mutation of the prothrombin gene discovered eight years ago during a work-up for an elevated activated protein C resistance ratio obtained for life-insurance underwriting; he has never required long-term anticoagulation because, despite the mutation, he has had no episodes of leg swelling, calf pain, or imaging-confirmed pulmonary embolus and remains under periodic surveillance by hematology. He denies chronic lung disease, chronic heart-failure admissions, inflammatory bowel disorders, connective-tissue disease, or malignant diagnoses, and he has not undergone any other operative or endoscopic intervention in the past thirty days. There have been no falls, vehicular accidents, or skeletal injuries, and he has never been immobilized in a fiberglass cast or traction device. He explicitly notes that his calves remain the same size “within millimeters” when he measures them after exercise, and inspection today finds smooth, non-varicose skin without pitting edema, cord, or tenderness. He has never required a peripherally inserted central catheter, port, or dialysis access; today’s venous line is a solitary 18-gauge catheter in the right forearm placed by anesthesia. No first-degree relatives have experienced venous thromboembolism, and his wife, who is waiting in the hallway, confirms the absence of clotting events in their adult children. He has never received heparin for more than procedural flushes and has never experienced thrombocytopenia or unusual bruising. Medications this morning include the aforementioned antiplatelet agents, amlodipine 5 mg, and vitamin D 1000 IU; he takes no hormone supplements, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or selective estrogen receptor modulators. He quit a 30-pack-year smoking habit twenty years ago, drinks a small bourbon on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Review of systems is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg heaviness with standing, abdominal pain beyond his known colonic disorder, neurologic deficits, or recent systemic infection apart from the resolved pneumonia. On examination he sits upright on the trolley reading a newspaper; vital signs show temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 122/68 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats/min in regular rhythm, respirations 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Body mass index is 25 kg/m². Jugular venous contour is ≤3 cm above the sternal angle, the point of maximal impulse is at the fifth interspace mid-clavicular, heart sounds are crisp without additional murmurs, and lungs are clear bilaterally with good air entry. Abdomen is soft and nondistended, with mild right-sided tenderness over the ascending colon but no peritoneal signs; prior laparoscopic port scars are absent. Lower limbs reveal symmetrical circumferences, warm skin, palpable posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ bilaterally, and no dilated superficial veins or edema. Neurologic screen demonstrates intact cranial nerves, full strength in all extremities, and normal gait when he takes a few test steps down the corridor. Laboratory studies drawn at 05:00 show hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, platelets 215 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.2 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, AST 24 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an INR of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A 12-lead ECG an hour ago shows normal sinus rhythm at 75 beats/min with the previously documented inferior Q-waves but no acute ST-changes. Chest radiography performed yesterday as part of surgical clearance depicts clear lungs and normal cardiac silhouette. Airway assessment reveals a Mallampati class I view, three-finger thyromental distance, and full neck extension; anesthesia anticipates straightforward laryngoscopy if intubation becomes necessary. Sequential intermittent pneumatic compression sleeves are hooked to the foot of the stretcher but not yet activated, and no anticoagulant prophylaxis has been administered pending final sign-in and discussion among surgery, cardiology, and anesthesia teams regarding the timing of his next clopidogrel dose.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score adds points for qualifying patient and procedure factors:
- Age 74 (61–74 years): 2 points.
- Planned laparoscopic hemicolectomy lasting 2–3 hours (>45 minutes): 2 points. Count the procedure once.
- Pneumonia 26 days ago: serious lung disease within the past month, 1 point despite resolution.
- Myocardial infarction 12 days ago: acute MI within the past month, 1 point.
- Confirmed prothrombin gene mutation: inherited thrombophilia, 3 points even without prior VTE.
BMI is exactly 25, not >25. He is ambulatory, the adenoma is nonmalignant, the IV is peripheral, and there is no personal or family history of VTE. No additional factors score.
Total = 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 9.
Final answer: 9
